planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall so roots establish in cool weather before the mid-to-late season bloom.

directions: Formal double flowers open white with the outer third of each petal blushed delicate flesh-pink, carrying 80 to 90 petals on blooms averaging about 4 inches across in mid-to-late season. The cultivar was originated by K. Sawada in Crichton, Alabama, first blooming in 1953 and registered with the American Camellia Society in 1958. Growth is medium-paced with thick, finely serrate dark green leaves on an upright shrub. Grow in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil with filtered light and consistent moisture.

planting.note: Fall planting lets the slow, bushy root system settle in before spring bloom.

directions: Semi-double flowers are shell-pink streaked with deep carmine and bordered in white, measuring 3 to 4 inches across and opening mid to late season. The cultivar arose as a sport of 'Lady Vansittart' and was introduced in 1949 by J. S. Tormey of California. Growth is slow, upright, and bushy, with glossy, deeply serrated foliage. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade.

planting.note: Plant in fall in acidic, humus-rich soil to establish before the mid-to-late season flush.

directions: Formal double, medium-to-large flowers are pink marbled with white, blooming mid to late season. It is a stable variegated sport of 'L'Avvenire' named by Guichard Soeurs of Nantes, France, and catalogued in the 1890s; it is also traded under the synonyms 'Lalla Rookh' and 'Laurel Leaf'. Growth is slow and compact, with narrow, sharply serrate leaves. Grow in acidic, well-drained soil with afternoon shade.

planting.note: Fall planting suits this vigorous, large-growing heritage cultivar before its long winter-to-spring bloom run.

directions: Fully double, coral-rose flowers with lavender overtones average about 5 inches across and bloom over an unusually long season from midwinter into mid-spring. It arose as a chance seedling in Valdosta, Georgia, found by Mrs. H. Turner Brice and registered with the American Camellia Society in 1957. It grows into a substantial 8 to 10 foot shrub with medium green foliage, and a pink-and-white flecked variegated sport is also in commerce. Provide acidic, well-drained soil and dappled shade.

planting.note: Plant in fall so roots are established before the October-November bloom season.

directions: Fragrant, semi-double to peony-form blooms are soft pink to shell-pink suffused with antique white and centered with bright yellow stamens, opening in October and November. This large, erect, spreading sasanqua was named by Dr. Hume in 1955 for Mrs. J. W. Solomon of Wilmington, North Carolina. It tolerates heat, humidity, and brief drought once established, making it a dependable Southern garden shrub. Plant with morning sun and afternoon shade in acidic, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant in spring in cool-summer climates; this selection performs poorly south of zone 7.

directions: Valued for abundant bright red-purple immature cones produced at the branch tips each spring, contrasting with fresh lime-green new growth, before the cones droop and mature to brown by summer. This irregular, spreading, somewhat weeping form of Norway spruce has been known in cultivation since about 1890, arising as a spontaneous mutation near Uppsala, Sweden. It prefers cool summer climates and struggles in heat. Plant in full sun in evenly moist, well-drained, acidic soil.

planting.note: Site where its flattened mound shape can be seen up close, such as a rock garden or trough.

directions: An irregular, flattened-globose dwarf Norway spruce with dense, stiff branching and thick blue-green needles arranged radially around the stems. Growth is extremely slow and spreads more than it rises, and older plants often develop a shallow central depression reminiscent of a miniature bird's nest. It is a long-grown 19th-century dwarf selection still favored for rock gardens, troughs, and container specimens. It tolerates ordinary, even dry, well-drained soil and needs no regular pruning.

planting.note: Makes an excellent container or patio specimen in addition to garden planting.

directions: A narrow, cone-shaped sport of the classic Dwarf Alberta Spruce ('Conica') discovered at Iseli Nursery in 1978 by Don Howse, distinguished by a second flush of bright creamy-yellow new growth that appears at branch tips in midsummer before fading to green by fall. It grows more slowly than 'Conica' and holds a dense, formal cone shape with little pruning needed. Plant in full sun to light shade in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Tolerates alkaline soils and urban conditions better than most spruces.

directions: A compact selection of Serbian spruce with densely held, two-toned needles, glossy dark green above and silvery-white beneath, that flash silver in the wind. Young plants form a tidy, globose mound that gradually becomes more upright and conical as growth accelerates with age. It originated as a witch's broom found around 1930 at Goudkade Brothers Nursery in Boskoop, the Netherlands. Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil.

planting.note: Use as a groundcover or bright color accent in hot, dry sites.

directions: A low, spreading creeping juniper prized for electric chartreuse-to-lime-green juvenile foliage that deepens to burnished gold in winter. It arose as a yellow sport of 'Youngstown' and was selected for resisting the summer sunburn that often afflicts gold-foliaged junipers. It forms a slowly spreading mound useful in rock gardens and mixed borders. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it tolerates poor soils and some urban pollution.

planting.note: Good for shrub borders, mass planting, and loose informal topiary.

directions: An arching, fountain-shaped juniper with fine-textured, bright mint-green foliage that holds its color well through winter. It was introduced into commerce by Monrovia Nursery in 1961 and remains widely sold under that trade name. It is versatile for shrub borders, mass plantings, and foundation use. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and avoid overly wet sites, which invite root and twig blight.

planting.note: Light afternoon shade helps preserve the cream variegation in hot climates.

directions: A compact, flat-mounding sport of 'Blue Star' with steel-blue foliage flecked and tipped in creamy white, giving the plant a sparkling, variegated look through the growing season. It was selected in the early 1990s at a nursery in Boskoop, the Netherlands, and named for a local soccer club. The cream variegation can scorch in hot afternoon sun, so light shade helps preserve the color. Plant in well-drained soil and avoid heavy, wet sites.

planting.note: Shelter from drying winter winds, which can brown the foliage.

directions: A naturally rounded, dense dwarf arborvitae that holds its globose form without shearing or pruning, one of the oldest and most dependable globe-form conifers in cultivation. The soft, aromatic, scale-like foliage is rich green through the growing season and takes on a slight bronze cast in winter. It is useful as a foundation planting, low hedge, or rounded accent. Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Good in rock gardens, foundation plantings, and perennial borders as a slow-growing specimen.

directions: A densely branched, irregularly flattened-globose dwarf eastern white pine with short, soft, lime-green needles. It was found as a natural dwarf in the 1950s by Bill Horsford near Charlotte, Vermont, and introduced to the nursery trade by Kate Brook Nursery in the early 1960s, making it one of the classic dwarf white pine selections in American gardens. It remains slow-growing and dense for decades with minimal care. Grow in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil.

planting.note: A favorite subject for bonsai training as well as rock gardens and small-space landscapes.

directions: A bushy dwarf Japanese white pine with short, twisted, blue-green needles held on an irregular, windswept-looking framework that matures into a broad pyramidal mound. It was selected in Scotland during the 1980s and 1990s by John Proudfoot of Methven. Its naturally sculptural habit and slow growth make it well suited to small gardens and container culture. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil.

planting.note: An occasional hand-cleaning of shed interior foliage keeps the pom-pom form crisp.

directions: A narrow, irregularly upright dwarf Hinoki cypress with tightly twisted, congested tufts of bright green foliage that create a distinctive pom-pom texture prized in Japanese-style gardens and bonsai. Older plants naturally shed small amounts of interior brown foliage. It was selected as a seedling in the mid-1970s by Joe Reis of Merritt, Long Island, New York. Grow in full to mostly sun with consistent moisture in rich, well-drained, acidic soil.

planting.note: Grown for dramatic winter silhouette value as much as summer foliage.

directions: An upright, tangled shrub form of Hinoki cypress whose branches and twigs twist and contort, with tips occasionally fusing into fan-shaped mutations. The dark green, scale-like foliage stays richly colored year-round. Growth is slow, eventually reaching small-tree stature at full maturity. Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; once established it tolerates considerable drought.

planting.note: Give full sun for the strongest gold color, with afternoon shade in the hottest climates.

directions: A slow-growing, broadly mounding dwarf falsecypress with cascading, thread-like branchlets in bright golden-yellow that hold their color through all four seasons. It is a more compact counterpart to the larger 'Filifera Aurea', valued for rock gardens, foundation plantings, and containers where space is limited. It is highly tolerant of urban pollution and adaptable to a wide range of soils. Plant in full sun for best gold color.
